an3.36:1.1: The three “messengers of the gods” here are a sick man, an old man, and a dead man. Buddhist traditions usually reckon the number as four, with the addition of a renunciate who inspires the spiritual path. This is the story told originally of Bodhisatta Vipassī ([dn14:1.31.1]()), and later of Gotama. Five are noted in [mn130](), with the addition of a baby and a man being punished. At [mn83:4.6]() the messengers are grey hairs. | In the Vedic tradition, the original messenger was Agni, the visible presence of divinity among humanity, brought from the fiery sun down to earth in the lightning (eg. Rig Veda 3.54.19,  5.26.6, 10.98.2). Other divinities might play a similar role, such as the wind (Atharva Veda 4.13.3). Later literature envisaged literal messengers sent to convey important information.
an3.36:1.5: The true role of Yama (“twin”, with his incestuous sister Yamī)is as guardian to the paths or rivers that lead one from one life to another ([sn1.33:10.3](), [mn130:3.1](), [dhp235]()). As the son of Vivasvant (the sun) and brother of Manu, he was born immortal but chose mortality. As the first person to die, Rig Veda 10.4 tells us that he discovered the paths to the lands of the dead that he now guards with his pair of hounds. Yama is a righteous god, but sinners see him as horrifying due to their own guilt (Brahma Purāṇa 106.46).
an3.36:17.4: Note: BB translates as if the hell itself covers 100 leagues, but usually to “pharati” is to “pervade” with some radiation, such a metta, etc. Here I think it means that the heat of the Great Hell pervades the surrounding regions.
an3.36:19.2: _Māṇava_, which normally means “Vedic student”, is occasionally used in the poetic sense of _manussa_ (“humans”). Both words mean “descendant of the first man, Manu”.
